newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK democrats attack China's plan on liberties.
newsitem.headline: HK democrats attack China's plan on liberties.

text.p: Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp on Sunday condemned Beijing's plan to dilute civil liberties in the territory after it returns to Chinese rule this year.

"The scrapping of the provisions will seriously dampen Hong Kong people's rights of freedom of speech, assembly, protesting and demonstrations," Democratic Party vice-chairman Yeung Sum was quoted as saying in the English-language Hong Kong Standard.

The 150-member China-appointed Preparatory Committee, which is overseeing Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule, on Saturday approved a Beijing plan to roll back civil liberties in the territory after it takes over on July 1.
The proposal would amend the territory's Bill of Rights Ordinance and repeal a number of other laws allowing public protests and association with foreign political organisations.
Yeung said his party, which holds the most seats in Hong Kong's current elected Legislative Council, would introduce a motion in the legislature condemning the Preparatory Committee's decision.

Independent legislator Emily Lau urged Chinese leaders on Sunday to take a more "relaxed attitude" toward Hong Kong, blaming China's moves to exert more control over the territory on leadership wrangling in Beijing.
"With the post-Deng Xiaoping transition still in a state of flux, apparently there are no strong leaders in Beijing who dare to take a relaxed attitude," Lau told the Hong Kong government radio.
"Consequently, they all would rather err on the side of being over-cautious. Thus, they would have maximum control," she said.

Hong Kong, ending more than a century and a half of colonial rule, will return to Chinese control on July 1. China has promised Hong Kong that the territory will maintain a high degree of autonomy and keep its capitalist way of life intact for 50 years after the handover.
Lau also called on the territory's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, to "learn to speak for the Hong Kong people rather than to be just a mouthpiece of Beijing".
The Preparatory Committee's proposal will now go to China's National People's Congress, or parliament, for ratification in March.
An opinion survey published on Sunday found most Hong Kong people appear to be against China's plan to roll back civil liberties.
The telephone poll, by the independent watchdog Hong Kong Policy Viewers, found 54.8 percent of 573 respondents were against Beijing's proposal, survey organisers said.
